newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia appears to waver on mining proposals.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia appears to waver on mining proposals.

text.p: Indonesia's Mines and Energy Ministry appeared to have done an about-turn on Monday over controversial changes to regulations governing the mining industry.
Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana told reporters after a meeting of economic ministers that the proposed changes were not final.
"They are still being discussed at the lower levels (of the ministry). They have not come to me yet," he said.
The ministry summoned mining companies last Tuesday and told them the new rules, which included a mandatory free 10-percent stake in mining ventures to the government, were non-negotiable.

They were given until July 1 to respond to the proposals, which would change the seventh-generation contracts of work (COW) already approved by the government and signed by mining companies. The COW is vital for mining operations.

By last Thursday, when coal miners were called in, mining sources said the heavy-handed approach had eased off. "The general feeling now is that it probably will be negotiable -- if in fact it is put into effect at all," one source said on Monday.
"This looks like a 180-degree about-turn," another said.
Asked about current laws that allow 100 percent foreign owned companies to operate in Indonesia, Sudjana said: "We will just follow the law."
Well informed sources within the government said that despite Sudjana's comments, the original directive had come down "from a high level".
"They did come down from a high level with a firm directive that they (the proposals) were not negotiable," one source said.
Mining and economic analysts said the original directive had placed foreign investment in Indonesia in jeopardy.
"It is doing a lot of damage, and not just in the mining industry," one source said.

The proposals as put to the mining industry last week included the mandatory 10 percent allocation to the government, and a stipulation that mining companies with operations in Indonesia would have to share capital gains made on stock exchanges outside the country with their shareholders.
In addition, raising additional capital through a public offering of shares would have to be done in Indonesia.

The proposals, which analysts said had a distinctly nationalistic flavour, followed the world's worst mining scandal. What was believed to be a huge gold discovery on Borneo island turned out to be a fraud earlier this year.
Mining analysts said the confusion should start to clear in the next few days.

"The biggest quandary is whether it has been a major exercise in kite flying, to test the waters to see how much they can get away with. Or whether the proposals represent a determined change of direction at the cabinet level," a senior analyst said.
But a senior mining source said it appeared the proposals had been put together without consulting other government ministries.
"The impression is that it's very ill thought out and not likely to get very far," he said, adding that foreign mining firms were likely to halt exploration work if the proposals were enforced.

Industry sources said some companies were putting up a united front to the proposals, while companies had also been advised to take legal action if necessary to enforce the seventh-generation COWs already approved and signed.
